polynesian_tangaroa.name: Beget the fish and the reptiles
polynesian_tangaroa.notes: Through his son Punga, Tangaroa is grandfather of Ikatere (ancestor of fish, who went to the sea) and Tū-te-wehiwehi/Tū-te-wanawana (ancestor of reptiles, who fled inland), so that the war between Tangaroa and his brother Tūmatauenga continues as humans fishing his offspring.

sources.reference: Te Ara: The Encyclopedia of New Zealand, 'Tangaroa – the sea'

polynesian_tangaroa.name: Take the form of whale, shark and other sea creatures
polynesian_tangaroa.notes: As the grand atua of the ocean Tangaroa is manifested in and as the great sea-creatures — whale, shark, stingray and eel.

sources.reference: Te Ara: The Encyclopedia of New Zealand, 'Tangaroa – the sea'

polynesian_tawhirimatea.name: Beget the winds and the cloud-hosts
polynesian_tawhirimatea.notes: To make war on his brothers for separating their parents, Tāwhirimātea fathered an army of winds and clouds — Apū-hau ('fierce squall'), Apū-matangi, and the cloud-children Ao-nui, Ao-roa, Ao-pōuri and the rest — and dispatched a wind-child to each quarter (tūāraki north, tonga south, marangai east, hauāuru west).

sources.reference: Te Ara: The Encyclopedia of New Zealand, 'Tāwhirimātea – the weather'

polynesian_tawhirimatea.name: Hurl thunder, lightning, hail and snow
polynesian_tawhirimatea.notes: Atua of the whole tempest: rain, hail, snow, cloud, wind, thunder and lightning are his to send.

sources.reference: Te Ara: The Encyclopedia of New Zealand, 'Tāwhirimātea – the weather'

polynesian_tumatauenga.name: Master and source of warfare
polynesian_tumatauenga.notes: Tūmatauenga is the origin and patron of war; rituals over warriors before battle, and the dedication of a male infant to a fighting role, invoked Tū as the source of their martial duty.

sources.reference: Te Ara: The Encyclopedia of New Zealand, 'Traditional Māori religion – ngā karakia a te Māori'

polynesian_taranga.name: Bear and name the five Māui brothers
polynesian_taranga.notes: Mother of the Māui brothers; having borne the last prematurely she wrapped him in the tress of her topknot and cast him to sea, whence his name Māui-tikitiki-a-Taranga ('Māui of the topknot of Taranga').

sources.reference: Sir George Grey, Polynesian Mythology (1855), 'The Legend of Maui'

polynesian_whaitiri.name: Sit blind in the sky counting her taro and kūmara
polynesian_whaitiri.notes: Returned to the heavens after her marriage to the mortal Kaitangata; there she went blind and was found by her grandsons Tāwhaki and Karihi at the foot of the vines of ascent, endlessly counting the tubers that are her only food until Tāwhaki restored her sight.

sources.reference: Sir George Grey, Polynesian Mythology (1855), 'The Legend of Tawhaki'

polynesian_whiro.name: Devour the dead in the underworld
polynesian_whiro.notes: The dead descend to Whiro, who consumes them and grows stronger with each, a power that fuels his unending enmity with Tāne of the light.

sources.reference: Elsdon Best, The Maori (1924), vol. 1, on Whiro and the lower world

polynesian_wahieroa.name: Carry the name of paternal vengeance
polynesian_wahieroa.notes: Named 'Long-piece-of-firewood' by Tāwhaki to commemorate his revival-by-fire after the cousin-attack and to encode the duty of vengeance; killed by the ogre Matuku(-takotako/-tangotango) while fetching a pregnancy-craving food (tūī birds) from the monster's preserve, the death his son Rātā is bound to avenge.

sources.reference: Sir George Grey, Polynesian Mythology (1855), 'The Legend of Rata'

pomo_coyote.name: Bring fire and the arts of living to the people
pomo_coyote.notes: Beyond his trickster role, Coyote is the culture-hero who gives essential gifts — fire, daylight, song and storytelling — and teaches humankind the customs of civilization.

sources.reference: S. A. Barrett, 'A Composite Myth of the Pomo Indians,' Journal of American Folklore (1906)

pomo_kuksu.name: Appear as the Big Head healing-spirit of the dance
pomo_kuksu.notes: In ritual Kuksu is the masked 'Big Head' spirit impersonated in the ceremonial house; his impersonator, body painted black or striped red-white-black and crowned with a bulky feather headdress, performed the curing dances of the Kuksu system.

sources.reference: E. M. Loeb, The Western Kuksu Cult, University of California Press (1932)

pomo_marumda.name: Teach the people their customs and crafts
pomo_marumda.notes: In the de Angulo/Benson cosmology 'Old Man' Marumda is the one who taught the Pomo nearly everything they know and practice; he deliberates over humanity drawing on his long stone tobacco-pipe.

sources.reference: Jaime de Angulo & W. R. Benson, Eastern Pomo creation narrative (de Angulo, 'Pomo Creation Myth,' Journal of American Folklore, 1935)

pomo_ragno.name: Spin the line that rescues the creators
pomo_ragno.notes: As the spider-grandmother 'Old Mother,' Ragno repeatedly rescues the creators Marumda and Kuksu from their own deluge and world-fire.

sources.reference: Jaime de Angulo & W. R. Benson, Eastern Pomo creation narrative (de Angulo, 'Pomo Creation Myth,' Journal of American Folklore, 1935)

pukawiss.name: Originate the hoop dance and the dances of the animals
pukawiss.notes: Watching the eagles, birds and snakes he loved, Pukawiss mimicked their movements and fashioned hoops to form the hoop dance, becoming the people's first dancer, performer and storyteller — a teacher of the animals' ways.

sources.reference: Basil H. Johnston, Ojibway Heritage (1976)

redhorn.name: Make living human heads grow on his earlobes
redhorn.notes: Redhorn makes faces/living human heads grow on his earlobes (or earbobs that come to life when worn); their laughing at the giants' woman spoils her play and wins the contest for his side.

sources.reference: Paul Radin, The Winnebago Tribe (1923); 'Redhorn Cycle' (Hocąk)

purepecha_xaratanga.name: Shape-shift and govern childbirth and fertility
purepecha_xaratanga.notes: Moon goddess who could change her form and who presided over fertility, childbirth, love and pulque; propitiated by her people in these matters.

sources.reference: Relación de Michoacán (c. 1540), on Xarátanga

purepecha_auicanime.name: Trick a mother into cooking her own child
purepecha_auicanime.notes: Disguised as an old woman she deceived the wife of Hopótacu into cooking her infant son Zinziani under pretext of a shared meal, bringing famine-tragedy and divine retribution — the act that fixes her as the malevolent counter-power to Cuerauáperi.

sources.reference: Relación de Michoacán (c. 1540), on Auicanime

rapanui_haua.name: Master the sea-bird flocks as Chief of the Eggs
rapanui_haua.notes: With Makemake, Haua drove the nesting sea-birds to the islets Motu Nui and Motu Iti; appearing to a priestess the two founded the birdman cult, and the first eggs of the season were dedicated 'for Haua, for Makemake.'

sources.reference: Alfred Métraux, Ethnology of Easter Island, Bishop Museum Bulletin 160 (1940)

rapanui_hiro.name: Send the rain as his own weeping
rapanui_hiro.notes: God of wind and rain; the rain was held to be his tears, summoned in drought by chanting 'E te uá, matavai-roa a Hiro-é' ('O rain, great tears of Hiro') and by sounding the stone trumpet Pu o Hiro.

sources.reference: Alfred Métraux, Ethnology of Easter Island, Bishop Museum Bulletin 160 (1940)

rapanui_uoke.name: Lever up the lands and sink them into the sea
rapanui_uoke.notes: The primeval giant levered up the lands one by one with his huge pole and let them sink; reaching Rapa Nui his pole broke against the rock, leaving only this last fragment of earth standing — the island's own account of its small size and the name Te Pito o te Henua, 'the fragment of the earth.'

sources.reference: Thomas Barthel, The Eighth Land (Das achte Land, 1974), on Uoke and Manuscript E

rapanui_tangaroa.name: Flesh that will not cook in the earth-oven
rapanui_tangaroa.notes: Come from Hiva in the shape of a seal with a human face and voice, Tangaroa was killed and placed in the umu; though baked the full time his flesh would not cook, proving him a chief of great mana.

sources.reference: Alfred Métraux, Ethnology of Easter Island, Bishop Museum Bulletin 160 (1940)

polynesian_tumatauenga.name: Offering of the first-slain (te mata-ika)
polynesian_tumatauenga.notes: Tūmatauenga received te mata-ika, 'the face of the fish' — the first enemy killed in battle — dedicated to him; warriors and male infants were ritually dedicated to him as the source of their fighting role.

sources.reference: Te Ara: The Encyclopedia of New Zealand, 'Traditional Māori religion'; 'Traditional Māori warfare – riri'

pomo_kuksu.name: Kuksu dance (Big Head ceremony)
pomo_kuksu.notes: In the semi-subterranean dance house an initiate impersonated Kuksu/Guksu — body painted, in a great feather headdress — to perform the curing dances of the secret Kuksu society.

sources.reference: E. M. Loeb, The Western Kuksu Cult, University of California Press (1932)

rapanui_haua.name: Tangata-manu (birdman) egg festival
rapanui_haua.notes: At Orongo the yearly contest for the first sooty-tern (manutara) egg from Motu Nui was held for Haua and Makemake; the gathered eggs were dedicated 'for Haua, for Makemake,' and the eight cult-deities' names were chanted by the competitors.

sources.reference: Alfred Métraux, Ethnology of Easter Island, Bishop Museum Bulletin 160 (1940)

rapanui_hiro.name: Rain-summoning with the Pu o Hiro
rapanui_hiro.notes: In drought the ariki paka, in ceremonial dress, sounded the pierced stone trumpet Pu o Hiro and chanted 'E te uá, matavai-roa a Hiro-é' to call the wind-and-rain god to weep his rain upon the land.

sources.reference: Alfred Métraux, Ethnology of Easter Island, Bishop Museum Bulletin 160 (1940)

roman_acca_larentia.name: Larentalia
roman_acca_larentia.notes: Public festival on 23 December at which sacrifice (parentatio, an offering to the dead) was made at her tomb in the Velabrum; in the aetiology she bequeathed her wealth to the Roman people and was honoured as mother of the original Arval Brethren (Fratres Arvales).

sources.reference: Varro, De Lingua Latina VI.23–24; Plutarch, Romulus 4–5; Macrobius, Saturnalia I.10; Aulus Gellius, Noctes Atticae VII.7

purepecha_curicaueri.name: Offering of tobacco and blood to the perpetual fire
purepecha_curicaueri.notes: His chief offerings were tobacco (thrown into the fire as rolled pellets, whose smoke pleased him), blankets, and the blood of bloodletting cast into the flames; warriors painted themselves black in his honour, re-enacting the sun's nightly battle with the stars.

sources.reference: Relación de Michoacán (c. 1540), on Curicaueri

purepecha_cuerauaperi.name: Pilgrimage and offerings at Zinapécuaro
purepecha_cuerauaperi.notes: Her hilltop sanctuary at Zinapécuaro drew pilgrims for fertility rites and offerings imploring rain and increase from the mother of the gods.

sources.reference: Relación de Michoacán (c. 1540), on Cuerauáperi

attributes.name: Arms outstretched lifting the sky
attributes.notes: Carvings and depictions show Tāne with outstretched arms holding the sky apart from the earth, his defining cosmogonic act.

sources.reference: Te Ara: The Encyclopedia of New Zealand, 'Tāne – the forest'

attributes.name: Storm-clouds, wind and lightning
attributes.notes: Represented by the cloud-hosts, gale-winds and lightning that are his children and weapons.

sources.reference: Te Ara: The Encyclopedia of New Zealand, 'Tāwhirimātea – the weather'

attributes.name: Embodiment of darkness and decay
attributes.notes: The dark antithesis of Tāne's light, dwelling in Taiwhetuki the House of Death where illnesses and black arts are kept.

sources.reference: Elsdon Best, The Maori (1924), vol. 1, on Whiro

sacredAnimals.name: Lizard / reptile
sacredAnimals.notes: Whiro-te-tipua is figured in reptilian form, the giant lizard embodying lurking, stealthy evil.

sources.reference: Elsdon Best, The Maori (1924), vol. 1, on Whiro

attributes.name: Long-Nosed God maskette / Morning Star figure
attributes.notes: Identified iconographically with the long-nosed-god maskettes and the Morning Star figure of Mississippian shell and Picture-Cave art, marked by the red scalp-lock and the human heads worn as earrings.

sources.reference: Robert Hall, An Archaeology of the Soul (1997); R. Diaz-Granados et al., Picture Cave (2015)

attributes.name: Crescent moon on the forehead
attributes.notes: Shown as a moon goddess with a crescent at her brow and a skirt of feathers.

sources.reference: Purépecha deity iconography after the Relación de Michoacán (Seler; Corona Núñez)

sacredAnimals.name: Serpent
sacredAnimals.notes: In the Relación, priests who misused her adornments and wine were turned into snakes and buried themselves, linking her with serpents and the subterranean passage to rebirth.

sources.reference: Relación de Michoacán (c. 1540), on Xarátanga

attributes.name: Sacred stone; figure painted black with heron plumes
attributes.notes: In the Relación he appears as a white eagle with a wart on the forehead, as a black-painted figure crowned with white heron down on head and back, and most often simply as the stone that is the god himself.

sources.reference: Relación de Michoacán (c. 1540), on Curicaueri

sacredAnimals.name: Eagle
sacredAnimals.notes: Descends and travels the cosmos as a white eagle (also as coyote and serpent).

sources.reference: Relación de Michoacán (c. 1540), on Curicaueri

attributes.name: Staring face or skull with great round eyes
attributes.notes: The most frequent figure in Easter Island rock art, carved as a wide-eyed face or skull (the mata-large masks at Orongo's Mata Ngarahu).

sources.reference: Alfred Métraux, Ethnology of Easter Island, Bishop Museum Bulletin 160 (1940); Bradshaw Foundation, 'The Birdman Motif of Easter Island'
